Prescription for Addiction

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In Benoni, the street dealer wears a white coat.

Unique Selling Point:
Undercover footage of us going to two pharmacies and a doctors clinic who sell medications without prescription.

Summary:
Legal drugs. Illegal deals. A quiet town hooked in plain sight.
Benoni, Gauteng — best known for its suburban calm and scenic lakes — is hiding a dangerous epidemic. Pharmacies and a private clinic are fuelling widespread addiction by handing out high-risk Schedule 4, 5, and even Schedule 7 drugs with no prescriptions, no oversight, and no accountability. This is a story of legal drugs being sold illegally, and it’s happening daily in full view of the community.
We went undercover. We filmed it. We found the people whose lives have been destroyed by it. And what we uncovered will leave you stunned.
The Investigation:
Lakefield Pharmacy (RingPharm Network)
• Previously exposed in 2017 by Benoni City Times and reported on as far back as 2008.
• Owned by Dr Sello Mashamaite (About Page)
• Undercover Purchase: Sold us Stilpane (Schedule 5) — a codeine- and meprobamate-based painkiller known on the street as green beans.
• Offered an unlabelled "very strong cough mixture" containing Celestamine, a Schedule 4 steroid-antihistamine — no prescription, no receipt.
Westwood Pharmacy
• Sold us Stilnox (Zolpidem) (Schedule 4) — a potent sleeping tablet — without a prescription.
• Owned by Mr Rufus Theunis Terblanche and Mr Riaaz Gani (LinkedIn)
LJM Medical Clinic – “The Pethidine Clinic”
• Run by Dr Jean Marc Lomena Mukombola, a Congolese doctor and pastor (Facebook, YouTube)
• Locals say the clinic is administering daily pethidine drips — a Schedule 7 opioid normally reserved for severe hospital use.
• We were told we’d need to “go in” to receive treatment.
• Dr Mukombola allegedly makes house calls, administering pethidine outside clinical settings.
Case Studies: Real People, Real Harm
"Peter" – Brother-in-Law Hooked on Pethidine
• His relative receives daily Pethidine drips at LJM Medical Clinic.
• Describes the clinic as “full of people leaving on a high.”
• Doctor allegedly falsifies receipts as “sinus treatment.”
• The patient was in a car accident post-treatment and remembers nothing.
• Peter is willing to speak anonymously with voice disguise.
"Joe" – Son Addicted, Brother Dead
• Joe’s brother died from addiction, now his teenage son is hooked on prescription sedatives from Lakefield and Westwood.
• He begged the pharmacy to stop supplying — they refused.
• Claims his son is being charged 3x the normal price because there's no prescription.
• Joe will speak on record.
"Ashley" – Husband Lost to Stilnox
• Her husband became addicted to prescription drugs from a Benoni pharmacy.
• She personally bought Stilnox without a prescription — as confirmed by our footage.
“They hand it over like it’s cough syrup. No ID, no questions. Just cash.”
• She is scared to speak publicly but willing to contribute off-record.
Experts
Dr Eugene Allers – Psychiatrist (On Record)
• Has seen a rise in addiction to codeine, sleeping pills, tranquilizers — all sourced “legally.”
• Several of his patients are directly connected to these pharmacies and the clinic.
Dr Field – Local GP (Off Record)
• Confirms the crisis is real.
• Refuses to stock morphine or oxycodone:
“We won’t touch morphine or oxy’s. The risks are just too high.”
• Warns that pharmacies are charging 200%+ markups to profit from addiction.
This is not a fringe drug story — this is a middle-class suburb where doctors and pharmacists are the dealers. Legal drugs are fuelling addiction under the radar, and nobody’s watching.
• Addiction Rising: Benzodiazepines, opioids, and codeine-based cough syrups are leading the trend.
• System Failure according to SAHPRA: No national prescription tracking. “Pharmacy hopping” goes unchecked. Codeine Care tracking initiative still not fully implemented.
Video Evidence: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1RaU9NcUq6Z_ecdM8WxS94F6Dr_RMY18I


Further information:
Summary: Prescription Drug Regulation & Abuse in South Africa
Rising Addiction
Prescription drug abuse is increasing, particularly involving benzodiazepines, opioids (e.g. codeine, pethidine), and codeine-based cough syrups. This is driven by poor regulation, patient demand, and unethical providers. Corruption and theft also play a role.

Dispensing Laws
Strictly regulated by the Medicines Act, Pharmacy Act, and Good Pharmacy Practice:

Schedules 5 & 6 require valid prescriptions and recordkeeping.

Max 30-day supply; Schedule 6 cannot be repeated.

Schedule 7 drugs (like pethidine) are highly restricted and typically hospital-only.

Monitoring Gaps
There is no national tracking system, enabling “pharmacy hopping.”
Initiatives like Codeine Care aim to address this but are still in rollout phases.

Online Risks
Unregulated online sales are growing, providing access to falsified, unregistered, or prescription-free drugs. SAHPRA works with law enforcement to clamp down.

Penalties for Violators
Illegal dispensing can lead to criminal charges, fines, suspension, or deregistration by SAHPRA, SAPC, or HPCSA.

Script:


SCRIPT: "Prescription for Addiction"
In Benoni, the street dealer wears a white coat.
OPENING SEQUENCE – “THIS IS BENONI”
Visuals: Benoni visuals - schools, busy roads, shopping centres.
VO: This is Lakefield, a suburb of Benoni — on Johannesburg’s East Rand.
[Pause. Visual shift: Inverted transition]
Within just a one-kilometre radius, almost any scheduled medicine is up for grabs — no script required… you just need to know where to go… and who to ask.
Quick cuts: Drip visuals, addict, pills, pharmacy visuals, payment…
PRESENTER LINK: Addiction in Benoni doesn’t look like we expect. It’s not needles in alleyways. It’s pills in medicine cabinets. And it's being fueled by doctors and pharmacists.
Visuals: Benoni
VO: Little did we know, our investigation into prescription addiction would lead us to a doctor who literally locked us inside his practice. Turns out, getting out was harder than getting the drugs.
Dr Mukombola: You don’t go, you don’t go!
[Fade to Black]

ACT 1 – THE UNDERCOVER EXPOSE
Visuals of Dr Allers
Dr Eugene Allers: In Benoni we have a problem, that pharmacies, one in particular, give out medicines and scheduled medicines without prescriptions. It’s illegal.
VO: Psychiatrist Dr Eugene Allers has seen it daily for more than two decades — patients addicted to meds from local pharmacies. It often starts with codeine — which, in many cases, doesn’t even need a script.
Dr Allers: So in South Africa, we estimate about 12% of the population being addicted to codeine.
VO: But in Benoni, it’s nearly five times higher.
Dr Allers: 52% of the patients that come to our hospital are addicted to codeine.
VO: Opioids like Codeine, which turns into morphine in the body, are strong painkillers — effective in the short-term, but highly addictive with repeated use.
Dr Allers: People become addicted. And then it starts giving you the pain. And the same with morphine. You take too much, and the next day you have a hangover, which is pain, then people take more morphine more to treat that pain, but it’s in actual fact the previous day's morphine that gave you the pain.
VO: After codeine, come heavier hitting drugs — like Stilpane or Stilnox.
Dr Allers: In our clinic, patients they take up to fifty per day. It numbs the emotions, but it also gives you a sense of euphoria.
VO: They’re all highly addictive. All Schedule 4 and above. All supposed to be controlled by prescription.
[Visual Shift: Inverted transition] PAUSE
LINK: We’ve been chasing this story for years —and it's always been very difficult to get people to speak up, and now we understand why. In Benoni, they’re dependent on these doctors and pharmacists.
VO: In a town where cash is tight and doctors often unaffordable - are locals turning a blind eye to keep the meds coming?
Visuals: Simon intro sequence…
Simon: Buying Stilnox in this area is so easy; it's like buying Smarties.
VO: This man has a relative hooked on the sedative Stilnox. He’s asked us to keep him anonymous.
Simon: He could take between four to six tablets a night of Stilnox.
Govan: Jeez, that'll knock you out hey!
Simon: And then he'll wake up in the night and take another two or three, and that's how addicted he is.
Benoni shots…Lakefield pharmacy intro
VO: Is this a case of so-called healing hands creating addiction in the name of profit?
Lakefield Pharmacy: it's not a back-alley operation, it's an ordinary pharmacy in a mall. But it’s been on Carte Blanche’s radar for nearly 20 years.
[Hidden camera footage starts]
VO: We go undercover.
Producer: I just wanted to look at some cough mixtures.
VO: Cough syrup containing codeine is a popular choice among addicts. Our producer is led straight to the prescription counter, where a patient usually has to produce a doctor’s prescription.
Subtitle: Producer: Do I need a prescription?
Subtitle: Employee: No.
VO: But we want something stronger. So our producer uses the code she’s been told this “dealer” will understand.
Producer: I’ve hurt my back, so I wanted to get some Stilpane.
VO: Stilpane — a Schedule 5 painkiller containing codeine that needs a script.
Subtitle: Pharmacist: You said Stilpane? How many?
Subtitle: Producer: Ten, please.
VO: R40 for ten tablets — double the usual price.
Subtitle: Cashier: I can’t give you this one [receipt].
VO: No receipt means there’s no reportable record of the transaction.
Visual: undercover footage
VO: We go back several times and walk out with powerful prescription tranquilisers; Xanax and Valium.
Eugene Allers: Drug dealers sell drugs to make money, now if you're a pharmacy, and you become a drug dealer, clearly your interest is the same.
**prescription pad motif visual***

ACT 2 – THE CLINIC OF DEPENDENCE
Visual: Map and Dr John Mukombola cutout

PRESENTER LINK: South Africa doesn’t have a proper mechanism to track how many schedule medicines are distributed, which means it is a system open to abuse, and is being taken advantage of.
VO: We’re trying it out - right across the road. This is the practice of Dr John Mukombola. but around here, locals call him something else: "The Pethidine Doctor."
VO: Pethidine is a powerful opioid, listed under Schedules 6 and 7 — meant for short-term, in-hospital care.
But Dr Mukombola provides drips to patients in his own rooms.

Our sources claim this doctor deliberately hooks patients on pethidine - and then feeds the addiction.

Simon: The new thing in the area is the pethidine drips. They go complain of a bit of pain and he puts them on a drip, puts in the pethidine.

VO: In fact our source says it was a pethidine drip that really got his relative hooked.

Simon: He got his first hit and it was amazing and kept going back daily.
Govan: The person prescribing it knew that they would get an addict out of the situation?
Simon: It's all about the money.

VO: Our source says Mukombola even does house calls.

Simon: They’ve gone to the house to administer the pethidine and left him there almost in an unconscious state and then they leave.

Pause…Benoni Visuals
PRESENTER LINK: We sent our producer into this small suburban clinic, with just over a R1,000, and we wanted to see how much schedule medicine she can get. [Undercover footage begins]
VO: Inside: we spot the doctor, sitting in the waiting room… [pause] Our producer is led past other patients on drips… [pause] into a room with a bed and, of course, a drip stand.
Producer: I’ve had quite a lot of back pain, and I’m struggling to sleep.
Dr Mukombola: So, I'd like us to do one X-ray.
VO: No questions about other medications or conditions - no detailed history at all. Instead, minutes later — the producer is told she has a serious injury.
Technician: I think there’s a small fracture here.
PRESENTER LINK: Just for the record — our producer has no such injury. But I suppose he had to find “something”.
Dr Mukombola suggests an anti-inflammatory injection - but he’s quick to offer a stronger option.
Producer: And the injection?
Dr Mukombola: I’ll give you a strong injection. I’ll mix two things
Producer: Okay.
Dr M: If I give you pethidine, you won’t drive…
Producer: What is pethidine?
Dr Mukombola: It’s one of the strong painkillers.
VO: A strong, highly addictive opioid offered to a new patient with almost no questions asked.
Producer: I can come get the drip then later.
Dr Allers: If you start using it, giving patients drips or injections, you are going to make them addicted to the medicine.

VO: Dr Mukombola says his 24-hour practice leaves no time for house calls.

Undercover footage:
Producer: Do you do house calls?
Dr Mukombola: These days I’m too busy, I don’t do house calls.

VO: On her way out, the doctor gives our producer even more meds from a cardboard box.

Dr Mukombola: One [tablet] two times Tramadol.

[Sequence of Govan seeing meds with producer]
Govan: Did he offer to give you a pethidine drip?
Producer: Yes.
Govan: So it's real.
VO: We walk out with three scheduled drugs — and an offer of pethidine. These aren't Panados, but a potent, addictive cocktail.
Govan: So these should be prescribed: This is a steroid, this is a Codeine, and this is a pain med.

Visual transition into facebook window and then we go into the video…
VO: On Youtube, we find that the doctor is apparently also a pastor...
Upsound Dr Mukombola: Healing is your responsibility.
Healing bodies and saving souls… one drip and one sermon at a time… rudi says the transition needs to speed up
Govan: Do you think they getting people purposefully addicted?
Simon: I do think so. It's not cheap - it's R2500 at a time.
Govan: So these people are drug dealers?
Simon: Yeah.

VO: It’s time to ask the doctor whether he’s a healer — or a drug dealer?

Govan: Why are you dispensing pethidine at the clinic, when it should be dispensed at the hospital?
Dr Mukombola: I don’t dispense pethidine. I give to my patients.
Govan: You give to your patients?
Dr Mukombola: If they are in pain.
Govan: You dispensed medication on the basis of a so-called healed fracture, and there was nothing there?
Dr: No, no, no! Which patient is that?
Govan: The producer for Carte Blanche.
Dr: No, no. I don't do so.
Govan: We’ve recorded it on undercover footage.
Dr: I don’t do so. If the patient said to me she is sick, we address the problem. I don't do fraud. I do the right things.
Govan: You've been accused of trying to get people addicted to profit off of it?
Dr: No, I don't do like that. So, maybe you went to the wrong doctor. In the whole of Benoni, I'm Dr John. Dr John. I'm the best doctor here!
VO: Cue the conspiracy theories…
Dr Mukombola: In my practice, I test patients for pethidine. I know many people around here, because of the work that I’m doing, they are trying to sabotage it.
VO: As we try to leave, the doctor moves to close the door — trapping us inside.

Govan: What exactly are you doing now?
Dr Mukombola: So, why did you record? Why did you record me? You’re not supposed to record me.
Govan: I came here to give you a right of reply…
Dr: I did answer you.
Govan: At any point you could have asked me to leave…
Dr: Let's let law enforcement... Because you are breaking my right - I do have a right.
VO: Eventually we manage to open the door… then the patients, perhaps nervous of being outed as addicts, ask us to leave….
Patients: Please can you go? Can you go? Just go! Ja, go, go, go! Away with you! Go!
Govan: Thank you so much…
Transition… Benoni visuals
VO: We discover later that Dr Mukombola does have a dispensing licence - so why was he so insistent in denying that he dispenses the very medication our producer walked out with?
Dr Allers: If the doctor is a cause of an addiction, then that’s totally unethical. That's complete unethical behaviour.

ACT 3 – ADDICTION'S FOOTPRINT
Govan: Many people you think are using this?
Simon: There are thousands in the area. There are various pharmacies that are doing it

VO: Back to Lakefield Pharmacy where we'd scored potentially addictive medicines earlier. But, when we go looking for the owner, he’s not available. Pharmacist Dr Patel is. Wearing sunglasses, he seems to know the heat is coming…

Govan: We’ve been investigating this pharmacy for selling medication without prescriptions
Dr Patel: No, we don't do that.
Govan: Yes you do, we’ve been able to buy schedule 4 and up medicine?
Dr Patel: We're not allowed to give without a prescription.

VO: But his answers — like the missing scripts — just don’t add up.

Govan: How can you see that schedule, for schedule 4, 5 medication is being dispensed and the stock number is lowering and yet you don't have the matching prescriptions?
Patel: Exactly. Because I was not aware of it. Thanks for your time.[shakes hand]
Govan: Thanks Dr Patel.

VO: Under pressure, Dr Patel abruptly ends the conversation.

Visuals of benoni

VO: The Pharmacy Council says it is also investigating Lakefield Pharmacy — but action is on hold pending the outcome of a court case.

Simon: A woman died a week ago and the husband is investigating, and accusing one of the pharmacies of giving these drugs to his late wife.
PRESENTER LINK: We spoke to one doctor whose had enough and is refusing to prescribe opioids, maybe it’s time we all did?
Closing Montage: Govan walking out of shot
THE END.

TEASER 1: VO: It starts with a sore back… and a pill to take the edge off. Then another. And before they know it, they’re not treating the pain — they’re feeding the addiction.
Dr Allers: We see many of them, more than once a day.
Subtitle: Pharmacist: You said Stilpane? How many? Producer: Ten, please.

TEASER 2: VO: A stressed population, a health system out of reach, and pharmacies willing to play along
Producer: Do I need a prescription?
Employee: No.
VO: It’s the perfect storm for addiction. And here in Benoni, it’s already hit.
TEASER 3: No street dealers. Just trusted pharmacists and doctors.
Govan: So these should be prescribed: This is a steroid, this is a Codeine, and this is a pain med.
Are you in pain?
Producer: No.
VO: In Benoni, addiction wears a smile... and a name tag.

0000-00-00 Script: SCRIPT: "Prescription for Addiction" In Benoni, the street dealer wears a white coat. OPENING SEQUENCE – “THIS IS BENONI” Visuals: Benoni visuals - schools, busy roads, shopping centres. VO: This is Lakefield, a suburb of Benoni — on Johannesburg’s East Rand. [Pause. Visual shift: Inverted transition] Within just a one-kilometre radius, almost any scheduled medicine is up for grabs — no script required… you just need to know where to go… and who to ask. Quick cuts: Drip visuals, addict, pills, pharmacy visuals, payment… PRESENTER LINK: Addiction in Benoni doesn’t look like we expect. It’s not needles in alleyways. It’s pills in medicine cabinets. And it's being fueled by doctors and pharmacists. Visuals: Benoni VO: Little did we know, our investigation into prescription addiction would lead us to a doctor who literally locked us inside his practice. Turns out, getting out was harder than getting the drugs. Dr Mukombola: You don’t go, you don’t go! [Fade to Black] ACT 1 – THE UNDERCOVER EXPOSE Visuals of Dr Allers Dr Eugene Allers: In Benoni we have a problem, that pharmacies, one in particular, give out medicines and scheduled medicines without prescriptions. It’s illegal. VO: Psychiatrist Dr Eugene Allers has seen it daily for more than two decades — patients addicted to meds from local pharmacies. It often starts with codeine — which, in many cases, doesn’t even need a script. Dr Allers: So in South Africa, we estimate about 12% of the population being addicted to codeine. VO: But in Benoni, it’s nearly five times higher. Dr Allers: 52% of the patients that come to our hospital are addicted to codeine. VO: Opioids like Codeine, which turns into morphine in the body, are strong painkillers — effective in the short-term, but highly addictive with repeated use. Dr Allers: People become addicted. And then it starts giving you the pain. And the same with morphine. You take too much, and the next day you have a hangover, which is pain, then people take more morphine more to treat that pain, but it’s in actual fact the previous day's morphine that gave you the pain. VO: After codeine, come heavier hitting drugs — like Stilpane or Stilnox. Dr Allers: In our clinic, patients they take up to fifty per day. It numbs the emotions, but it also gives you a sense of euphoria. VO: They’re all highly addictive. All Schedule 4 and above. All supposed to be controlled by prescription. [Visual Shift: Inverted transition] PAUSE LINK: We’ve been chasing this story for years —and it's always been very difficult to get people to speak up, and now we understand why. In Benoni, they’re dependent on these doctors and pharmacists. VO: In a town where cash is tight and doctors often unaffordable - are locals turning a blind eye to keep the meds coming? Visuals: Simon intro sequence… Simon: Buying Stilnox in this area is so easy; it's like buying Smarties. VO: This man has a relative hooked on the sedative Stilnox. He’s asked us to keep him anonymous. Simon: He could take between four to six tablets a night of Stilnox. Govan: Jeez, that'll knock you out hey! Simon: And then he'll wake up in the night and take another two or three, and that's how addicted he is. Benoni shots…Lakefield pharmacy intro VO: Is this a case of so-called healing hands creating addiction in the name of profit? Lakefield Pharmacy: it's not a back-alley operation, it's an ordinary pharmacy in a mall. But it’s been on Carte Blanche’s radar for nearly 20 years. [Hidden camera footage starts] VO: We go undercover. Producer: I just wanted to look at some cough mixtures. VO: Cough syrup containing codeine is a popular choice among addicts. Our producer is led straight to the prescription counter, where a patient usually has to produce a doctor’s prescription. Subtitle: Producer: Do I need a prescription? Subtitle: Employee: No. VO: But we want something stronger. So our producer uses the code she’s been told this “dealer” will understand. Producer: I’ve hurt my back, so I wanted to get some Stilpane. VO: Stilpane — a Schedule 5 painkiller containing codeine that needs a script. Subtitle: Pharmacist: You said Stilpane? How many? Subtitle: Producer: Ten, please. VO: R40 for ten tablets — double the usual price. Subtitle: Cashier: I can’t give you this one [receipt]. VO: No receipt means there’s no reportable record of the transaction. Visual: undercover footage VO: We go back several times and walk out with powerful prescription tranquilisers; Xanax and Valium. Eugene Allers: Drug dealers sell drugs to make money, now if you're a pharmacy, and you become a drug dealer, clearly your interest is the same. **prescription pad motif visual*** ACT 2 – THE CLINIC OF DEPENDENCE Visual: Map and Dr John Mukombola cutout PRESENTER LINK: South Africa doesn’t have a proper mechanism to track how many schedule medicines are distributed, which means it is a system open to abuse, and is being taken advantage of. VO: We’re trying it out - right across the road. This is the practice of Dr John Mukombola. but around here, locals call him something else: "The Pethidine Doctor." VO: Pethidine is a powerful opioid, listed under Schedules 6 and 7 — meant for short-term, in-hospital care. But Dr Mukombola provides drips to patients in his own rooms. Our sources claim this doctor deliberately hooks patients on pethidine - and then feeds the addiction. Simon: The new thing in the area is the pethidine drips. They go complain of a bit of pain and he puts them on a drip, puts in the pethidine. VO: In fact our source says it was a pethidine drip that really got his relative hooked. Simon: He got his first hit and it was amazing and kept going back daily. Govan: The person prescribing it knew that they would get an addict out of the situation? Simon: It's all about the money. VO: Our source says Mukombola even does house calls. Simon: They’ve gone to the house to administer the pethidine and left him there almost in an unconscious state and then they leave. Pause…Benoni Visuals PRESENTER LINK: We sent our producer into this small suburban clinic, with just over a R1,000, and we wanted to see how much schedule medicine she can get. [Undercover footage begins] VO: Inside: we spot the doctor, sitting in the waiting room… [pause] Our producer is led past other patients on drips… [pause] into a room with a bed and, of course, a drip stand. Producer: I’ve had quite a lot of back pain, and I’m struggling to sleep. Dr Mukombola: So, I'd like us to do one X-ray. VO: No questions about other medications or conditions - no detailed history at all. Instead, minutes later — the producer is told she has a serious injury. Technician: I think there’s a small fracture here. PRESENTER LINK: Just for the record — our producer has no such injury. But I suppose he had to find “something”. Dr Mukombola suggests an anti-inflammatory injection - but he’s quick to offer a stronger option. Producer: And the injection? Dr Mukombola: I’ll give you a strong injection. I’ll mix two things Producer: Okay. Dr M: If I give you pethidine, you won’t drive… Producer: What is pethidine? Dr Mukombola: It’s one of the strong painkillers. VO: A strong, highly addictive opioid offered to a new patient with almost no questions asked. Producer: I can come get the drip then later. Dr Allers: If you start using it, giving patients drips or injections, you are going to make them addicted to the medicine. VO: Dr Mukombola says his 24-hour practice leaves no time for house calls. Undercover footage: Producer: Do you do house calls? Dr Mukombola: These days I’m too busy, I don’t do house calls. VO: On her way out, the doctor gives our producer even more meds from a cardboard box. Dr Mukombola: One [tablet] two times Tramadol. [Sequence of Govan seeing meds with producer] Govan: Did he offer to give you a pethidine drip? Producer: Yes. Govan: So it's real. VO: We walk out with three scheduled drugs — and an offer of pethidine. These aren't Panados, but a potent, addictive cocktail. Govan: So these should be prescribed: This is a steroid, this is a Codeine, and this is a pain med. Visual transition into facebook window and then we go into the video… VO: On Youtube, we find that the doctor is apparently also a pastor... Upsound Dr Mukombola: Healing is your responsibility. Healing bodies and saving souls… one drip and one sermon at a time… rudi says the transition needs to speed up Govan: Do you think they getting people purposefully addicted? Simon: I do think so. It's not cheap - it's R2500 at a time. Govan: So these people are drug dealers? Simon: Yeah. VO: It’s time to ask the doctor whether he’s a healer — or a drug dealer? Govan: Why are you dispensing pethidine at the clinic, when it should be dispensed at the hospital? Dr Mukombola: I don’t dispense pethidine. I give to my patients. Govan: You give to your patients? Dr Mukombola: If they are in pain. Govan: You dispensed medication on the basis of a so-called healed fracture, and there was nothing there? Dr: No, no, no! Which patient is that? Govan: The producer for Carte Blanche. Dr: No, no. I don't do so. Govan: We’ve recorded it on undercover footage. Dr: I don’t do so. If the patient said to me she is sick, we address the problem. I don't do fraud. I do the right things. Govan: You've been accused of trying to get people addicted to profit off of it? Dr: No, I don't do like that. So, maybe you went to the wrong doctor. In the whole of Benoni, I'm Dr John. Dr John. I'm the best doctor here! VO: Cue the conspiracy theories… Dr Mukombola: In my practice, I test patients for pethidine. I know many people around here, because of the work that I’m doing, they are trying to sabotage it. VO: As we try to leave, the doctor moves to close the door — trapping us inside. Govan: What exactly are you doing now? Dr Mukombola: So, why did you record? Why did you record me? You’re not supposed to record me. Govan: I came here to give you a right of reply… Dr: I did answer you. Govan: At any point you could have asked me to leave… Dr: Let's let law enforcement... Because you are breaking my right - I do have a right. VO: Eventually we manage to open the door… then the patients, perhaps nervous of being outed as addicts, ask us to leave…. Patients: Please can you go? Can you go? Just go! Ja, go, go, go! Away with you! Go! Govan: Thank you so much… Transition… Benoni visuals VO: We discover later that Dr Mukombola does have a dispensing licence - so why was he so insistent in denying that he dispenses the very medication our producer walked out with? Dr Allers: If the doctor is a cause of an addiction, then that’s totally unethical. That's complete unethical behaviour. ACT 3 – ADDICTION'S FOOTPRINT Govan: Many people you think are using this? Simon: There are thousands in the area. There are various pharmacies that are doing it VO: Back to Lakefield Pharmacy where we'd scored potentially addictive medicines earlier. But, when we go looking for the owner, he’s not available. Pharmacist Dr Patel is. Wearing sunglasses, he seems to know the heat is coming… Govan: We’ve been investigating this pharmacy for selling medication without prescriptions Dr Patel: No, we don't do that. Govan: Yes you do, we’ve been able to buy schedule 4 and up medicine? Dr Patel: We're not allowed to give without a prescription. VO: But his answers — like the missing scripts — just don’t add up. Govan: How can you see that schedule, for schedule 4, 5 medication is being dispensed and the stock number is lowering and yet you don't have the matching prescriptions? Patel: Exactly. Because I was not aware of it. Thanks for your time.[shakes hand] Govan: Thanks Dr Patel. VO: Under pressure, Dr Patel abruptly ends the conversation. Visuals of benoni VO: The Pharmacy Council says it is also investigating Lakefield Pharmacy — but action is on hold pending the outcome of a court case. Simon: A woman died a week ago and the husband is investigating, and accusing one of the pharmacies of giving these drugs to his late wife. PRESENTER LINK: We spoke to one doctor whose had enough and is refusing to prescribe opioids, maybe it’s time we all did? Closing Montage: Govan walking out of shot THE END. TEASER 1: VO: It starts with a sore back… and a pill to take the edge off. Then another. And before they know it, they’re not treating the pain — they’re feeding the addiction. Dr Allers: We see many of them, more than once a day. Subtitle: Pharmacist: You said Stilpane? How many? Producer: Ten, please. TEASER 2: VO: A stressed population, a health system out of reach, and pharmacies willing to play along Producer: Do I need a prescription? Employee: No. VO: It’s the perfect storm for addiction. And here in Benoni, it’s already hit. TEASER 3: No street dealers. Just trusted pharmacists and doctors. Govan: So these should be prescribed: This is a steroid, this is a Codeine, and this is a pain med. Are you in pain? Producer: No. VO: In Benoni, addiction wears a smile... and a name tag.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Undercover footage of us going to two pharmacies and a doctors clinic who sell medications without prescription.
metadata.Summary: Legal drugs. Illegal deals. A quiet town hooked in plain sight. Benoni, Gauteng — best known for its suburban calm and scenic lakes — is hiding a dangerous epidemic. Pharmacies and a private clinic are fuelling widespread addiction by handing out high-risk Schedule 4, 5, and even Schedule 7 drugs with no prescriptions, no oversight, and no accountability. This is a story of legal drugs being sold illegally, and it’s happening daily in full view of the community. We went undercover. We filmed it. We found the people whose lives have been destroyed by it. And what we uncovered will leave you stunned. The Investigation: Lakefield Pharmacy (RingPharm Network) • Previously exposed in 2017 by Benoni City Times and reported on as far back as 2008. • Owned by Dr Sello Mashamaite (About Page) • Undercover Purchase: Sold us Stilpane (Schedule 5) — a codeine- and meprobamate-based painkiller known on the street as green beans. • Offered an unlabelled "very strong cough mixture" containing Celestamine, a Schedule 4 steroid-antihistamine — no prescription, no receipt. Westwood Pharmacy • Sold us Stilnox (Zolpidem) (Schedule 4) — a potent sleeping tablet — without a prescription. • Owned by Mr Rufus Theunis Terblanche and Mr Riaaz Gani (LinkedIn) LJM Medical Clinic – “The Pethidine Clinic” • Run by Dr Jean Marc Lomena Mukombola, a Congolese doctor and pastor (Facebook, YouTube) • Locals say the clinic is administering daily pethidine drips — a Schedule 7 opioid normally reserved for severe hospital use. • We were told we’d need to “go in” to receive treatment. • Dr Mukombola allegedly makes house calls, administering pethidine outside clinical settings. Case Studies: Real People, Real Harm "Peter" – Brother-in-Law Hooked on Pethidine • His relative receives daily Pethidine drips at LJM Medical Clinic. • Describes the clinic as “full of people leaving on a high.” • Doctor allegedly falsifies receipts as “sinus treatment.” • The patient was in a car accident post-treatment and remembers nothing. • Peter is willing to speak anonymously with voice disguise. "Joe" – Son Addicted, Brother Dead • Joe’s brother died from addiction, now his teenage son is hooked on prescription sedatives from Lakefield and Westwood. • He begged the pharmacy to stop supplying — they refused. • Claims his son is being charged 3x the normal price because there's no prescription. • Joe will speak on record. "Ashley" – Husband Lost to Stilnox • Her husband became addicted to prescription drugs from a Benoni pharmacy. • She personally bought Stilnox without a prescription — as confirmed by our footage. “They hand it over like it’s cough syrup. No ID, no questions. Just cash.” • She is scared to speak publicly but willing to contribute off-record. Experts Dr Eugene Allers – Psychiatrist (On Record) • Has seen a rise in addiction to codeine, sleeping pills, tranquilizers — all sourced “legally.” • Several of his patients are directly connected to these pharmacies and the clinic. Dr Field – Local GP (Off Record) • Confirms the crisis is real. • Refuses to stock morphine or oxycodone: “We won’t touch morphine or oxy’s. The risks are just too high.” • Warns that pharmacies are charging 200%+ markups to profit from addiction. This is not a fringe drug story — this is a middle-class suburb where doctors and pharmacists are the dealers. Legal drugs are fuelling addiction under the radar, and nobody’s watching. • Addiction Rising: Benzodiazepines, opioids, and codeine-based cough syrups are leading the trend. • System Failure according to SAHPRA: No national prescription tracking. “Pharmacy hopping” goes unchecked. Codeine Care tracking initiative still not fully implemented. Video Evidence: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1RaU9NcUq6Z_ecdM8WxS94F6Dr_RMY18I
